content: Two studies did not find a statistically significant association between having a rural background and practicing in rural areas. However, one study did report a statistically significant association between rural practice and rural training. Evidence for these findings comes from countries across high-, middle-, and low-income settings. The studies included cohort, case-control, retrospective, and serial quantitative analyses. Many of these studies reported a substantial positive effect of targeted admissions on recruitment and retention of health workers in rural areas. The follow-up periods in these studies ranged from three to 20 years and spanned countries of varying socioeconomic statuses across five of the six WHO regions. Although most studies focused on medical students, one study involving nursing students also demonstrated a significant positive effect. A study in the United States on the long-term retention of medical doctors with rural backgrounds found that 68% of graduates with rural backgrounds were still practicing in rural areas after 11–16 years, compared to 46% of those with non-rural backgrounds. In Norway, the Decentralized Nursing Education (DNE) program, established in 1990 at Tromsø University College, targeted rural students for part-time studies. This program resulted in 75% of graduates obtaining their first employment in community healthcare services. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) suggested that combining this policy with others, such as local training, rural exposure, or scholarship programs with obligated service schemes, could have additive effects. In the Philippines, the Ateneo de Zamboanga University School of Medicine, located in the predominantly rural Zamboanga Peninsula, implemented a policy of admitting local students. Over 90% of its graduates practiced in the Philippines, compared to the national average of 32%. Of these, 85% were retained in the Zamboanga region, with 50% practicing in rural and remote areas. The study also measured the impact of retaining their health workforce on infant mortality, concluding that infant mortality in the region decreased by 90% over 14 years, compared to a national average reduction of 50%. Rural primary and secondary education systems in some settings may be less developed than urban schools, potentially disadvantaging rural-background students in health worker education programs. The GDG emphasized the importance of buffering these disparities to ensure rural students can succeed in such programs. The WHO guideline on health workforce development strongly recommends targeted admission policies to enroll students with rural backgrounds in health worker education programs. Evidence consistently demonstrates that admitting students with rural backgrounds has a substantial positive effect on the availability of rural health workers. This effect is observed across short-, medium-, and long-term periods and across countries of varying socioeconomic statuses. Locating health worker education facilities, schools, and residency programs outside major cities has been shown to improve the recruitment and retention of graduates in rural and remote areas. Thirteen studies, mostly observational, demonstrated a positive effect of rural-based schools and programs on graduates’ choices to practice in rural locations. However, there is a possibility of a preselection effect, as institutions in rural areas may attract students already interested in rural practice. For example, the Rural Medical Scholars Program in the United States showed that rural undergraduate training was more strongly associated with rural practice than postgraduate training. Two Australian studies on medical graduates concluded that longer training periods in rural areas had a stronger influence on recruitment and retention in rural areas. The GDG noted that the costs of establishing, staffing, and maintaining rural education institutions are high, including expenses for buildings, maintenance, travel, human resources, and student accommodation. However, these investments may be cost-effective due to potentially large returns on investment. Community engagement is essential for the development of schools in rural areas. The GDG also highlighted that curriculum and recruitment must be oriented toward rural health to ensure the success of such interventions.
